prompt: Why is the orders table called `customer_order` and not `order`?
hint: Think of `ORDER BY`.

choices.text: Hibernate prefixes a table's name with the name of its package
choices.why: Hibernate derives a table name from the entity's class, not its package, and `@Table` names this one explicitly.

choices.text: `ORDER` is a reserved word in SQL
choices.why: Right. It is the `ORDER` of `ORDER BY`, so a table with that name would need quoting in every statement.

choices.text: PostgreSQL keeps a system table of its own called `order`
choices.why: There is no such system table; the clash is with the language's grammar, not with another table.

choices.text: Flyway refuses table names that are shorter than six letters
choices.why: Flyway runs the SQL it is given and imposes no naming rule; the `author` and `book` tables are short.

prompt: `OrderLine` stores its own `priceCents` instead of reading the book's price when an order is shown. Why?
hint: What happens to an old order when a price changes next month?

choices.text: Hibernate cannot follow a lazy `@ManyToOne` to read a field
choices.why: It can, inside a transaction; `OrderResponse.from` reads each line's book title that way.

choices.text: To avoid a join every time the catalogue lists its books
choices.why: Listing books never touches `order_line`; the copy is about orders, not the catalogue.

choices.text: So that a later price change does not rewrite what somebody paid
choices.why: Right. The line records the price at the moment of the order; the book's price is free to move afterwards.

choices.text: Because the price field of `Book` is private
choices.why: `Book` has a public `getPriceCents()`, and `Order.add` calls it to make the copy.

prompt: An order asks for two copies of a book that has one. Why does the bookshop answer `409` rather than `400`?
hint: Is anything wrong with the request itself?

choices.text: A `400` is reserved for what Bean Validation rejects
choices.why: No such reservation exists; `400` means the request itself is malformed or invalid, whoever finds out.

choices.text: The request is valid, and the shop's current state refuses it
choices.why: Right. The same request would succeed with more stock, which is what a conflict with the resource's state means.

choices.text: A `409` makes HTTP clients repeat the request on their own
choices.why: No client retries a `409` by itself; retrying an out-of-stock order would only fail again.

choices.text: Spring maps every `RuntimeException` to `409` by default
choices.why: Unhandled, a `RuntimeException` becomes a `500`; the `409` comes from the `@ExceptionHandler` in `ApiErrorHandler`.

prompt: A JDBC connection in autocommit mode runs a statement. What is the transaction?
hint: Lesson 9's code never asked for one.

choices.text: Everything the connection does until it is closed
choices.why: That would make every statement wait for the end of the connection to take effect; autocommit is the opposite.

choices.text: That one statement, on its own
choices.why: Right. Each statement commits as soon as it finishes, which is fine for one insert and wrong for an order.

choices.text: None: in autocommit mode PostgreSQL runs statements outside any transaction
choices.why: Every statement in PostgreSQL runs in a transaction; autocommit only makes each one its own.

choices.text: Everything done while one HTTP request is being handled
choices.why: JDBC knows nothing about HTTP requests; grouping by request is what `@Transactional` on a service does.

prompt: An order asks for one Dom Casmurro (5 in stock) and two Frankenstein (1 in stock). Hibernate sends the `update` for Dom Casmurro before `take` fails on Frankenstein. What is Dom Casmurro's stock afterwards?
hint: An update sent is not an update committed.

choices.text: 4, because the update reached the database before the failure
choices.why: It reached the database inside the transaction, and the rollback undid it.

choices.text: 5, because Hibernate cancels updates it has already sent
choices.why: Hibernate cannot take back a statement; the database undoes it because the transaction rolls back.

choices.text: 5, because the rollback undoes the whole transaction
choices.why: Right. Sent or not, nothing inside a rolled-back transaction stays.

choices.text: 4 until the application restarts, then 5
choices.why: The stock lives in the database, not in the application's memory; a restart changes nothing.

prompt: Which of these, coming out of `place`, make Spring roll the transaction back by default? Choose all that apply.
hint: Unchecked, checked, and what never leaves the method.

choices.text: `OutOfStockException`
choices.why: It extends `RuntimeException`, which rolls back.

choices.text: An `IOException` declared with `throws`
choices.why: A checked exception commits by default, unless `rollbackFor` names it.

choices.text: An `IllegalStateException`
choices.why: It is a `RuntimeException` too, so it rolls back like any other.

choices.text: An `OutOfStockException` caught inside `place`, which then returns normally
choices.why: Spring only sees what leaves the method; a normal return commits whatever was done.

choices.text: An `Error`, such as `OutOfMemoryError`
choices.why: Errors roll back as well as runtime exceptions.

prompt: A service method throws a checked `PaymentDeclinedException` and must not commit. The `@Transactional` attribute that names it is `___`.
hint: By default a checked exception commits.

prompt: `OrderController` asks for an `OrderService` in its constructor. What does Spring give it?
hint: Where does the transaction begin?

choices.text: The `OrderService` object, with transaction code compiled into `place`
choices.why: The class is compiled exactly as written; nothing is added to the method.

choices.text: A new `OrderService` for each request
choices.why: The bean is a singleton, as lesson 5 showed; the proxy wraps that one object.

choices.text: A proxy wrapped around it
choices.why: Right. The proxy begins and ends the transaction around each call that comes in from outside.

choices.text: The `JpaTransactionManager`, which forwards calls to the service
choices.why: The transaction manager is what the proxy asks to begin and commit; it is never injected in the service's place.

prompt: During `place`, the debug log shows `Participating in existing transaction` for a repository call. What happened?
hint: `PROPAGATION_REQUIRED`.

choices.text: The repository started a transaction of its own and committed it at once
choices.why: That is what `Creating new transaction` would say; this line says it joined.

choices.text: The repository joined the transaction `place` had begun
choices.why: Right. With the default propagation a call inside a transaction becomes part of it, so the rollback covers it too.

choices.text: The repository borrowed a second connection from the pool
choices.why: Joining uses the same connection; a second one is what `REQUIRES_NEW` costs.

choices.text: The repository ran with no transaction, because the service already had one
choices.why: It ran inside the service's transaction, which is the point of participating.

prompt: In the detour, `place` has no annotation and calls `placeAt`, which is `@Transactional`. Why does `placeAt` run without a transaction?
hint: Through what does the call to `placeAt` travel?

choices.text: `@Transactional` works only on methods the controller calls by name
choices.why: Any caller outside the bean would do; the controller is just the one caller here.

choices.text: A method with an `Instant` parameter cannot be proxied
choices.why: Parameter types make no difference to a proxy; called from another bean, `placeAt` would get its transaction.

choices.text: `place` calls it on `this`, and that call never passes through the proxy
choices.why: Right. The proxy only sees calls that come in from outside the object.

choices.text: Only the first annotated method in a class is read
choices.why: Every annotated method is read; `get` keeps its read-only transaction in the same class.

prompt: A refused order must leave a row in an audit table, written by another bean called from inside `place`, even though `place` rolls back. Which setting does the audit method need?
hint: It must commit whatever the caller does.

choices.text: `propagation = Propagation.REQUIRED`
choices.why: That joins the order's transaction, so the order's rollback takes the audit row with it.

choices.text: `readOnly = true`
choices.why: A read-only transaction is meant not to write at all, and it would still join the caller's.

choices.text: `isolation = Isolation.SERIALIZABLE`
choices.why: Isolation decides what concurrent transactions see, not whether this work survives a rollback.

choices.text: `propagation = Propagation.REQUIRES_NEW`
choices.why: Right. It suspends the order's transaction and commits its own, at the cost of a second connection.

prompt: Match each `@Transactional` attribute to what it does.
hint: Two of them are propagation.

pairs.right: joins the caller's transaction, or starts one
suspends the caller's transaction and commits its own
Hibernate skips dirty checking and never flushes
rolls back when the checked exception X leaves the method

right_distractors: runs the method again after a rollback

prompt: The bookshop never chose an isolation level. Which one does it run at?
hint: PostgreSQL's default.

choices.text: `REPEATABLE READ`
choices.why: That is MySQL's default, not PostgreSQL's.

choices.text: `SERIALIZABLE`
choices.why: It is the strictest level, and no common database starts there.

choices.text: `READ UNCOMMITTED`
choices.why: PostgreSQL accepts the name and runs it as `READ COMMITTED`; it is not the default either.

choices.text: `READ COMMITTED`
choices.why: Right. `SHOW transaction_isolation` answered `read committed`.

prompt: At `READ COMMITTED`, a transaction reads a book's stock twice. Between the two reads another transaction commits a change to it. What does the second read return?
hint: What does each statement see?

choices.text: The new, committed value
choices.why: Right. Each statement sees what was committed when it began: a non-repeatable read.

choices.text: The value the transaction saw first, because it holds one snapshot
choices.why: One snapshot for the whole transaction is `REPEATABLE READ`.

choices.text: Nothing until the other transaction's lock is released
choices.why: The other transaction has already committed, and a plain read never waits for a writer in PostgreSQL anyway.

choices.text: An error saying the row changed during the transaction
choices.why: Reads never fail this way; the serialization error comes at a write, and at a stricter level.

prompt: At `REPEATABLE READ`, `place` fails with `could not serialize access due to concurrent update`. What must the application do for the order to go through?
hint: The snapshot it read from is out of date.

choices.text: Repeat only the `update` that failed, in the same transaction
choices.why: The transaction is aborted; and its earlier reads came from the stale snapshot anyway.

choices.text: Run the whole transaction again from the start
choices.why: Right. A new transaction takes a new snapshot, reads the current stock and decides again.

choices.text: Nothing: PostgreSQL retries the transaction by itself
choices.why: PostgreSQL rolls it back and reports the error; the retry is the application's code.

choices.text: Lower the level to `READ UNCOMMITTED` for that one statement
choices.why: A level cannot change in the middle of a transaction, and in PostgreSQL that level is `READ COMMITTED`.

prompt: Without the lock, two orders for one copy each arrive together for a book with 1 in stock, and both are accepted. What does the book's stock read afterwards?
hint: Each transaction wrote what it computed from what it read.

prompt: Why did `CHECK (stock >= 0)` not stop the two orders for the last Frankenstein?
hint: Look at the value each `update` wrote.

choices.text: Neither write went below 0, so it never fired
choices.why: Right. Each write set the stock to 0; the second replaced the first instead of subtracting from it.

choices.text: Hibernate's `update` bypasses the table's constraints
choices.why: Constraints are checked by the database on every statement, whoever sends it.

choices.text: `READ COMMITTED` checks constraints only at the end of the day's work
choices.why: The isolation level has nothing to do with when a `CHECK` runs; it runs on each write.

choices.text: Flyway turned the constraint off when it applied `V3`
choices.why: Flyway ran the migration as written, and the constraint is in force.

prompt: With `findByIdForUpdate`, ana and bia order the last Frankenstein at the same moment and ana's read comes first. Put the events in order.
hint: The second locking read waits.
items: ana's transaction locks the row and reads 1
bia's transaction asks for the same row and waits
bia's transaction gets the row and reads 0
bia's transaction rolls back and bia gets a 409
trap: bia does not read 1 and then wait: the locking read itself is what waits.

prompt: Which change to `place` would make the lock on a popular book hurt the most?
hint: How long is the row held?

choices.text: Saving the order before the loop instead of after it
choices.why: The inserts move earlier but the transaction lasts about as long; the lock time barely changes.

choices.text: Calling a payment service between the locking read and the commit
choices.why: Right. Every order for that book queues behind the network call, each holding a connection.

choices.text: Marking `get` as `@Transactional(readOnly = true)`
choices.why: `get` reads orders without a locking read, so it does not touch the book's lock.

choices.text: Ordering two different books in one request instead of a single one
choices.why: Two rows are locked instead of one, each for the same short time.

prompt: Customers edit their own delivery address, and two edits of the same address almost never meet. Which protection against a lost update fits?
hint: Nobody should wait for a collision that rarely happens.

choices.text: A `@Version` column, with a retry when the update loses
choices.why: Right. Optimistic locking costs nothing until a collision, and then the losing edit is retried or reported.

choices.text: A `PESSIMISTIC_WRITE` lock on every read of an address
choices.why: It works, and makes every reader wait to guard against a collision that almost never happens.

choices.text: Raising the pool's `maximum-pool-size`
choices.why: More connections run more transactions at once, which makes collisions likelier, not rarer.

choices.text: Leaving it to `READ COMMITTED`
choices.why: The lost update is possible at `READ COMMITTED`; that is how two Frankenstein orders went through.

prompt: With `connection-timeout=5000`, how many seconds does a request wait for a free connection before it fails?
hint: The property is in milliseconds.

prompt: With a pool of two connections and one row locked by `psql`, the third of three orders failed after five seconds. Why the third?
hint: What were the other two doing while they waited?

choices.text: PostgreSQL refuses more than two transactions waiting on one locked row
choices.why: PostgreSQL queues any number of waiters; the third never reached the database at all.

choices.text: The two others held both connections while they waited for the lock
choices.why: Right. A transaction keeps its connection while it waits, so the pool was empty for the third.

choices.text: HikariCP lends connections only in the order the pool opened them
choices.why: The order of lending is not the issue; there was no free connection to lend.

choices.text: `connection-timeout` counts from when the application started
choices.why: It counts from when the request asked for a connection; the log said `timed out after 5005ms`.

prompt: In production the log shows `Connection is not available, request timed out` a few times an hour, at the busiest moments. What should be looked at first?
hint: What holds a connection for longer than it should?

choices.text: Raising `maximum-pool-size` to the database's `max_connections`
choices.why: One instance would then take every connection the database has, and more active queries than cores only slows each one.

choices.text: Raising `connection-timeout` to 30 seconds
choices.why: Requests would wait longer for the same shortage, and fail later instead of sooner.

choices.text: Which transactions last long, and what they wait on
choices.why: Right. An exhausted pool is usually transactions holding connections too long, as the one waiting on a lock did.

choices.text: Turning autocommit on for every connection in the pool
choices.why: That would break every order into separate commits and undo what the lesson built.

prompt: Which of these changes to the bookshop can leave a book's stock wrong without any error reaching the customer? Choose all that apply.
hint: Look for a commit that should have been a rollback, and for two writers.

choices.text: `place` catches `OutOfStockException` and returns the order without that line
choices.why: A normal return commits: lines taken before the failure keep their stock change, whatever the order says.

choices.text: `place` reads books with `findById` instead of `findByIdForUpdate`
choices.why: Two orders at once can both read the same stock and both be accepted: the lost update.

choices.text: `take` throws a checked exception declared on `place`, with no `rollbackFor`
choices.why: A checked exception commits by default, so earlier lines stay taken even though the customer sees an error for the order.

choices.text: `take` throws `OutOfStockException`, as it does now
choices.why: That is the lesson's code: the transaction rolls back and the customer gets a `409`.

choices.text: `maximum-pool-size` is lowered to 2
choices.why: A small pool makes requests fail with a `500`, which the customer sees; it does not change what a transaction writes.

prompt: Match each symptom to its cause.
hint: Every one of these appeared in the lesson.

pairs.left: two `201`s for the last copy, stock 0, two orders
pairs.right: a read with no lock before the write

pairs.left: a `500` after five seconds, `Connection is not available`
pairs.right: every connection held by a waiting transaction

pairs.left: `could not serialize access due to concurrent update`
pairs.right: a stricter level refusing a conflicting write

pairs.left: a `@Transactional` method that ran with no transaction
pairs.right: a call on `this` that skipped the proxy

right_distractors: a `CHECK` constraint refusing a negative stock

prompt: A new endpoint cancels an order and puts its copies back in stock. A double click sends two cancellations of the same order together, and both put the copies back. What prevents it?
hint: It is the lost update again, on a different row.

choices.text: Make the cancel method `@Transactional(readOnly = true)`
choices.why: A method that must write cannot be read-only, and the flag says nothing about other transactions.

choices.text: Set the cancel method's isolation to `READ COMMITTED` explicitly
choices.why: It already runs there, and that level lets both read the order as not cancelled.

choices.text: A locking read of the order, refusing one already cancelled
choices.why: Right. The second cancellation waits, then reads the order as cancelled and stops.

choices.text: Raise `maximum-pool-size` so that both cancellations run without waiting
choices.why: Running both at once without waiting is the problem, not the fix.

prompt: An order asks for one Dom Casmurro and two Frankenstein, of which there is one. Put what happens in order.
hint: The proxy is first and last.
items: the proxy around `place` creates a transaction
a locking read fetches Dom Casmurro
Hibernate sends the update of Dom Casmurro's stock
the proxy rolls the transaction back
trap: The update is sent before Frankenstein is read, because Hibernate flushes before the next query; it is still undone.
